title: Maintenance and support retainers
summary: What happens after launch: why apps break without code changes, what a support retainer covers, and how to keep a client's app, and its AI feature, healthy month after month.
youWillLearn: Why a launched app keeps breaking even when nobody touches the code
The difference between a warranty and a retainer
How monitoring and small, regular updates make support predictable
How to survive AI model retirements with one env var and an eval set

glossary.package: Code written by someone else that your app uses, such as a date picker or the database client.
glossary.warranty: A promise to fix defects in your own work for free, for a set period after launch.
glossary.retainer: A monthly agreement where the client pays a fixed fee for ongoing care and a set amount of your time.
glossary.SLA: Service level agreement: how fast you promise to respond and start work, usually by how severe the problem is.
glossary.uptime monitor: A service that loads a page of your app every few minutes and alerts you when it fails.
glossary.error tracking: A tool that collects crashes from your app, with the error message and where in the code it happened.
glossary.pull request: A proposed change to the code that you can review and test before it is merged into the live app.
glossary.Dependabot: A GitHub feature that watches your packages and opens pull requests when updates are available.
glossary.eval set: A fixed list of real inputs with known good answers, used to check an AI feature still works after a change.
glossary.offboarding: Ending a client relationship cleanly: removing your access, handing over loose ends and confirming it in writing.

steps.title: Sam's app, two months after launch
body: Sam owns a small hair salon. Two months ago you launched her booking app: clients book online and get a text reminder before each visit.
The app leans on outside things: packages (code written by others), an SMS service (a company that sends the texts) and billing, the card that pays for hosting.

scene.caption: The booking app works, leaning on packages, an SMS service and a paid hosting plan.

steps.title: Saturday: "Nobody can book"
body: A Saturday text from Sam: "Nobody can book." Your code did not change. The world around it did: the hosting card expired, the SMS service retired an old version, a package needed a security fix.
An app is less a finished painting, more a garden. Agree who tends it, how fast and for how much before that Saturday.
changes: ~ Booking App: broken, though its code did not change
~ SMS Service, Packages, Billing: each changed under it
~ First to know: Sam, on a Saturday

scene.caption: The code stayed the same. Things around it changed, and the app broke.

steps.title: Warranty first, then a retainer
body: After launch come two phases. First, the warranty from your contract: for a short period, defects in your own work are fixed for free.
Then a retainer: a monthly fee for keeping the app healthy, plus a little change work. Outside causes, like a provider retiring a version, are maintenance, inside the warranty or not.

callout.text: A new car. The warranty covers factory faults for a while. Oil changes, tires and brakes are servicing, paid for every time, no matter who built the car.

changes: − Sam, Booking App, Packages, SMS Service, Billing
+ Launch, Warranty, Retainer: the phases after the build

scene.caption: Launch, then a short free warranty, then an ongoing paid retainer.

steps.title: What a retainer actually buys
body: A retainer is not "call me whenever". Write it as a short list: monitoring, monthly updates, a backup check, a block of hours for small changes, and response times.
Those response times are your SLA, set by severity. A broken booking page on Saturday is not the same as a typo in the footer.

code.code:
Included:  monitoring, monthly updates, backup check,
           4 hours of small changes per month
Response:  P1 site down       reply within 4 business hours
           P2 feature broken  next business day
           P3 small change    planned for next month
Excluded:  new features (quoted separately),
           provider fees (paid by the salon)
Unused hours do not roll over.
code.caption: P1 is the most urgent. Write "reply within", not "fixed within": you control your reply, not every outside provider.

callout.text: Define "business hours" in writing. Saturday may be the salon's busiest day. If you do not work weekends, say so, or price weekend cover separately.

changes: ~ Retainer: a short written list, with reply times
~ Launch and Warranty fade back

scene.caption: The retainer is a short, written list, with response times by severity.

steps.title: Find out before Sam does
body: You cannot respond fast to problems you do not know about. Three cheap signals cover most small apps: an uptime monitor on the booking page, error tracking for crashes, and usage alerts from the hosting and AI providers.
The production module goes deeper. Here, the point is: monitoring is what makes your SLA honest.
changes: − Launch, Warranty, Retainer
+ Booking App, and You, who gets the alerts
+ Uptime Check, Error Tracking, Usage Alerts: three signals
~ First to know Sam → You

scene.caption: Three signals reach you before an angry text from Sam does.

steps.title: Updates arrive as small pull requests
body: Packages get fixes all the time. Yearly updates are one huge, scary jump. Boring, small, regular updates are the goal.

Dependabot, a GitHub feature, opens a pull request (a proposed change) for each update. The hosting builds a preview copy of the site from it. You check the preview, run the tests, and merge: the update goes live.

code.code:
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        patterns: ["*"]
        update-types: ["minor", "patch"]
code.caption: Grouping small updates into one pull request a week keeps the noise down.

changes: − Booking App, You, Uptime Check, Error Tracking, Usage Alerts
+ Dependabot, Pull Request: a robot proposes each update
+ Preview, Live Site: a test copy first, then the real app

scene.caption: An update becomes a pull request, gets a preview, and only then reaches the live site.

steps.title: AI models get retired
body: Say Sam later added AI rebooking: her app server (the computer running her code) asks a Claude model for ideas. Old models get retired, and then the feature breaks.
Two cheap habits: the model's name in one env var (a setting outside the code), and an eval set: about 20 real cases with good answers, run before every switch.

code.caption: Simple string checks are a start. The AI module covers stronger evals.

callout.text: When Claude Code switches the model for you, check: did it change only AI_MODEL, or quietly rewrite prompts too? Ask it to run the eval set before and after, and show failures side by side. Add the provider's deprecations page to your monthly checklist.

changes: − Dependabot, Pull Request, Preview, Live Site
+ App Server, Old Model: today's AI feature, model retiring
+ Model Setting: the model id, in one env var
+ Eval Set, New Model: real cases tested before the switch

scene.caption: The model id lives in one place. The eval set tests the new model before the switch.

steps.title: Pricing Sam's retainer
body: Price it from the time it really takes. Count a typical month: updates, checking monitors and backups, a few hours of changes, and a short monthly report.
Being reachable costs you time even in quiet months, so include it. Then offer two tiers: Care keeps the app healthy, Care Plus adds change hours and faster replies. Sam picks.

callout.text: Track your real hours for the first three months. If the retainer keeps running over, re-price it openly rather than quietly working for free.

changes: − App Server, Old Model, Model Setting, Eval Set, New Model
+ Monitoring, Updates: the Care tier
+ Change Hours, Faster Reply: added in Care Plus

scene.caption: Two clear tiers. The second adds change hours and a faster reply.

steps.title: Quick favors and forgotten access
body: Two slow leaks. First, the quick favor: five minutes here and there, untracked, until you work a free day each month. Log every task against the retainer hours and send Sam a short monthly report.
Second, when a retainer ends, do proper offboarding: remove your access everywhere, hand over anything new, and confirm it in writing.

callout.text: A monthly check with Claude Code: run npm audit (known security holes) and npm outdated (old packages), list the AI models in use, and summarize the month's changes for Sam's report. Read the summary before sending: it must not claim work you did not do.

changes: − Monitoring, Updates, Change Hours, Faster Reply
+ You, Monthly Report, Sam: logged work, reported monthly
+ Quick Favors, Old Access: the two slow leaks
~ Unpaid hours 0 → 6 a month

scene.caption: Logged work goes into a monthly report. Untracked favors and old access leak.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Apps break without code changes, because providers, packages and models keep moving. After a short warranty, a retainer pays for care: monitoring, small regular updates, a few change hours and clear reply times.
Keep the model id in one env var with an eval set ready, log every hour, and offboard cleanly when it ends.
changes: − Old Access: removed at offboarding
~ Quick Favors: now logged in the Monthly Report
~ Unpaid hours 6 → 0

scene.caption: Every favor is logged and reported. No access is left behind.

quiz.question: Four months after launch, the SMS service retires the version the app uses, and reminders stop. Sam's warranty was 30 days. Who pays for the fix?

options.text: You, because it is your code.
options.why: The code was correct when delivered. An outside provider changed; that is maintenance, not a defect in your work.

options.text: It falls under the retainer, or is quoted as maintenance if there is none.
options.why: Keeping up with outside changes is exactly what a retainer is for. Without one, it is new paid work.
Providers announce changes and expect customers to update. They will not fix your integration for you.

quiz.question: What makes a retainer's response time (SLA) believable?

options.text: Monitoring and alerts that reach you before the client notices.
options.why: You can only reply in four hours to problems you know about. Uptime checks and error tracking make the promise real.

options.text: Promising to fix every issue within four hours.
options.why: You cannot control every fix, for example when an outside provider is down. Promise a reply time, not a fix time.

options.text: Giving Sam your personal phone number.
options.why: It makes you reachable but not informed. Without monitoring, you still hear about problems last.

quiz.question: The provider announces it will retire the model Sam's AI feature uses. Claude Code offers to update the model id in seven files. What is the better setup?

options.text: Let it edit all seven files; it is fast.
options.why: It works once, but the next retirement repeats the hunt, and one missed file means a broken feature.

options.text: Never switch models, to avoid risk.
options.why: A retired model stops working. Not switching is not an option; switching safely is.

options.text: Read the model id from one env var and run the eval set before switching.
options.why: One place to change, and a quick test that the new model still gives good answers for Sam's real cases.

takeaways: Apps break without code changes: providers, packages and AI models keep moving.
A warranty covers your own defects for a short time. A retainer pays for ongoing care.
Write the retainer as a list: monitoring, updates, change hours, and reply times by severity.
Small weekly package updates through pull requests and previews beat one scary yearly upgrade.
Keep AI_MODEL in one env var and an eval set ready. Log every hour, and offboard in writing.
